theme: Genealogies from Adam through Judah’s line [survey]
readingInstruction: Read 1 Chronicles 1:1-2:55. This is a survey reading, so do not try to study every name. Read it as the opening of a story: the line from Adam to Abraham to Israel to Judah. Watch where the genealogy slows down.
settingTheScene: Chronicles was written for the returned community, probably after 400 BC, to answer a pressing question: are we still the people of God? The first book begins with nine chapters of genealogies, a surprising start. But to a people who had lost their kingdom, temple, and land, these lists said: you belong. The line from Adam never broke. Chronicles retells the history of Israel from Adam to the decree of Cyrus, focusing on David, the temple, and the hope of restoration. It is a different perspective from Samuel and Kings, which were written in exile.
observation: “The sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth” (1:4).
“The sons of Abraham: Isaac and Ishmael” (1:28).
“These are the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun” (2:1).
“The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, and Shelah” (2:3).
“Achan, the troubler of Israel, who broke faith in the matter of the devoted thing” (2:7).
“Jesse fathered Eliab his firstborn… David the seventh” (2:13-15).
interpretation:
The genealogy begins with Adam and moves quickly through the nations of the world. The Chronicler wants his readers to see that Israel’s story is part of the world’s story. All nations descend from Adam and Noah, and Israel is chosen out of them. Then the lists narrow: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the twelve sons.

Then the writer slows down on Judah, listing his sons and their descendants. Judah is the line of the king, and the lists lead toward David. The genealogy is not neutral. It is shaped to tell a story of promise. Even in the lists, we see grace: Tamar, who was wronged and acted, is named. Rahab, once a Canaanite prostitute, is in the line of Judah. Even Achan, the troubler, is remembered, a reminder that failure is part of the story.

Why include these names? In the ancient world, a genealogy was a kind of identity card. To the returned exiles, the names proved that they were not forgotten. Every name stands for a person known to God. The Chronicler’s point is that the promises to Abraham and David were still alive.

There is also a subtle emphasis on God’s choice. David is the seventh son of Jesse, the youngest, not the oldest. The one who was passed over by his own family is the one God chose. Throughout the Chronicles, the surprising pattern appears again and again: God chooses the unexpected.

As you read, do not feel lost in the names. Treat them like a family photo album. You do not need to know everyone in it, but you can feel that you belong to a story much bigger than yourself.
connection: Matthew 1:1-17 opens the New Testament with a genealogy of Jesus, including Tamar, Rahab, and Ruth. Luke 3:23-38 traces Jesus back to Adam. Luke 10:20 says to rejoice that your names are written in heaven. Philippians 4:3 speaks of names in the book of life. Revelation 21:27 mentions the Lamb’s book of life. Acts 17:26 says that God made from one man every nation.
application:
Take a few minutes to write the names of three generations of your family. Thank God for each.

Remember that you are known by name. Read Luke 10:20 aloud.

Notice God’s surprising choices, in Scripture and in your life.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that your name is known to him.
Thank him that no one is forgotten in his plan.
Ask him to keep you faithful to your place.
